s1: Lustre began as a research project in 1999. Peter Bram, then at Carnegie Mellon, built on ideas from the code of file system and its offshoot, Intermezzo. In 2001, he founded a company, Cluster File Systems, to build it. The money and the motivation came from the U.S. Department of Energy, through a program called ASCI Path Forward, which wanted a file system that could keep up with the supercomputers the labs were buying. In March 2003, Lustre went into production on a cluster at Lawrence Livermore, and version 1.0 followed that December. Two documents from this era are worth knowing. A November 2002 white paper from Cluster File Systems laid out the architecture. And a 2003 paper by Philip Schwann, at the Linux Symposium, describes building it for clusters of a thousand nodes. By then, Lustre was running on three of the eight largest clusters on the June 2003 top 500 list. Then ownership changed hands several times. Sun bought the company's assets in 2007, and Oracle inherited them. In December 2010, Oracle announced it would stop developing the two-point X-line. The developers formed WhamCloud, which Intel acquired in 2012. In 2018, DDN took over the Lustre team from Intel, and in 2019, the trademark passed to the user groups, Open SFS and EOFS, through all of that it stayed open source. By one count, more than 60 of the hundred fastest machines have used it since 2005, though I treat that number as approximate.
s2: Why build it this way? The 2003 paper gives a crisp argument. In a design where clients share raw disk blocks, locking of i-nodes and allocation maps happens at the block level, and the authors say that limits scaling to roughly a dozen or two nodes. So instead of exposing disks, Lustre exposes objects. A file is not a list of disk blocks. Its i-node, hooked on a metadata server, points to objects, and each object lives on some storage server, which decides for itself where to put the bytes on its own disks. That makes the division of labor clean. Metadata servers handle the namespace, names, directories, permissions, and the layout of each file. Object storage servers handle the data. A client asks the metadata server once, learns the layout, and then talks to the storage servers directly. Contrast that with the design from last time. There, any node can touch any disk, and nodes coordinate through tokens. Here, a storage target is served by one server at a time, so nobody has to coordinate over who writes a given block. The price is that there is now a specific place where metadata lives. Neither choice is free. Hold on to that trade-off, because it explains why so much of Lustre's story is about scaling and protecting the metadata side.
s5: Stripping buys performance. To keep it correct, Luster needs locks. The Luster distributed lock manager, the LDLM, makes sure that when one client writes in another reads, the reader sees the data the way it would on a local disk. Each lock is managed by a single server and in the 2003 design it never migrates between masters. Locks on a files data are managed by the storage servers that hold its objects. The paper makes a point of how small this is. The whole lock manager was just over 4,000 lines of code. Data locks cover byte ranges and here's a trick that should sound familiar. The server may grant a lock larger than the one requested. If you're the only client touching a file, you typically get a lock on the whole file and never ask again. When a conflicting request arrives, the server calls the holder back and the ranges are renegotiated. Metadata has its own trick, intent locks. Creating a file would normally take several steps. Look up the directory, take a lock, then create. With intent locking, the client sends its whole intention open or create in one request. The metadata server performs it and returns the result together with a lock if one is useful. The 2003 paper also describes choosing by contention. In a quiet directory, hand the client a lock so it can cache and batch changes, though the paper says that cache was still planned. In a hot directory like slash TMP, grant no lock at all. The server just does each operation itself because passing a lock back and forth would cost more than the work. Compare with GPFS. Both use by-trained locks with generous grants that shrink under contention. The real difference is where the lock state lives. Spread across token managers in GPFS, held by the server that owns the object in Lustre.
s6: Everything so far talks over a network and Lustre has its own layer for that. LNET. It gives the file system one messaging interface and underneath drivers called LNDs for each fabric. TCP over Ethernet, InfiniBand, Omnipath, Rocky and several proprietary ones. Every node has an address of the form. Address that network type called an ID. Servers listen on TCP port 988. LNET was originally based on the portals interface from Sandia, and it uses remote direct memory access where the hardware allows, so bulk data moves without the processor copying it. Networks don't always match, so LNET routers bridge one network to another. Frontiers file system, which we'll meet shortly, has 169 of them. And since version 2.10, multi-rail lets one node bundle several network interfaces into a fatter pipe. Bulk transfers have grown. The largest request was 4 megabytes in version 2.4, 16 in 2.9, and up to 64 megabytes in 2.13. My reading. The same story as block sizes. As disks and networks got faster, bigger requests were needed to amortize the fixed cost of each one. For perspective, in the 2003 paper, two nodes over Aquadrix Elan network moved over 300 megabytes per second, limited by the PCI bus. And one shared file scaled across 1100 nodes, the limit of the hardware they had. That was the frontier then.
s7: Back to the trade-off we flagged. With one metadata server, every create, stat, and rename in the whole system funnels through a single machine. Luster has attacked that bottleneck in layers. First, the distributed namespace environment, DNE. Version 2.4, in 2013, lets sub-directory trees live on different metadata targets. Later versions can spread one huge directory across targets, and the 2.15 defaults can place new directories round-robin or by free space. Second, small files. Opening and reading, a small file normally costs a trip to the metadata server, and then a trip to a storage server. Data on MDT from version 2.11 stores the first piece of a file right on the metadata target, which helps small files. Third, layouts that change as files grow. Progressive file layouts from version 2.10 let one file use different layouts for different regions. Narrow at the start, wider as it grows. File-level redundancy, a year later, added mirrored layouts for availability and read performance. Under all of it, targets are formatted with a local file system. Originally, that was L-disc FS, a modified X4. Since version 2.4, ZFS is supported too, with a much higher maximum file size. 8 exbibites against about 31 pebibites for L-disc FS. Failures are handled in pairs. A partner server can mount a dead server's targets. A client that goes silent is evicted after a timeout, by default 100 seconds. Its locks are revoked and its unwritten cached data is discarded. Eviction is the price of letting everyone else keep going. The documented limits show how far this has stretched. The 2003 paper's goal was tens of thousands of clients. Today's manual lists up to 8,150 targets, 256 metadata targets, and 131,000 clients, with more than 30,000 tested in production.
